article.title: Survivorship Bias: What You Miss When You Study Only Active Customers
article.why: Practical analytical English for data-driven decisions.

paragraphs.en: Customer analysis often begins with the people who are still visible: active members, current cardholders, recent purchasers, or users who continue to log in. This is convenient because their records are easy to find. It can also create survivorship bias. Customers who left, stopped purchasing, closed an account, or became unreachable may disappear from the analytical population even though their absence is exactly what the business needs to understand. Suppose a retailer studies satisfaction among customers who made a purchase this year. The remaining customers may report high satisfaction, but dissatisfied customers who stopped shopping are missing. The analysis can therefore overstate the health of the relationship. The same issue appears in product usage. If analysts calculate feature adoption only among users who remain active after six months, they exclude people who may have churned because the product was difficult to use. Financial analysis can suffer too: studying only accounts that remain open can make historical performance look stronger than the experience of the original cohort. Cohort design is one way to reduce the problem. Define a population at a clear starting point, such as everyone acquired in a given quarter, and follow all members over time. Customers who become inactive should remain part of the denominator when the question concerns retention. Analysts should distinguish between current-state questions and longitudinal questions. “What do today’s active customers look like?” legitimately focuses on survivors. “What happened to customers acquired last year?” requires the original cohort, including those who disappeared. Missingness itself can be informative. Analysts should investigate why records vanish and whether exit is related to the outcome being studied. Administrative rules matter as well. A customer may appear inactive because an ID changed or a channel was discontinued rather than because the relationship ended. Good reporting names the population explicitly and shows attrition through the funnel. Retention, churn, satisfaction, and customer value are especially vulnerable to survivorship bias because the least successful relationships are often the first to disappear from convenient datasets. Looking only at those who remain can answer a useful question, but it is not the same question as understanding everyone who started. Analysts should state the population, observation window, assumptions, and decision point before interpreting the result. A useful review separates the observed pattern from the mechanism that may have produced it and from the action that should follow. This discipline makes the analysis easier to reproduce, challenge, and communicate to stakeholders. paragraphs.zh: 繁中完整翻譯與解說：本文重點是不要讓單一摘要數字、留下來的樣本、模型選擇結果或統計調整取代對資料生成機制的理解。分析時要先界定母體、時間點、selection mechanism 與真正要回答的 business question，再判斷觀察到的差異可以支持到什麼程度。
paragraphs.ja: 日本語完全訳・解説：単一の要約値、生き残ったsample、modelによるselection、統計的な調整だけでdata generating processを置き換えて考えないことが重要である。母集団、時点、selection mechanism、business questionを先に定義し、観察された差がどこまでの結論を支持できるかを判断する。
